title: In Caravaggio’s Calling of Saint Matthew in Rome, a single beam of light does the pointing
body: Caravaggio (Michelangelo Merisi) painted *The Calling of Saint Matthew* in 1599–1600 for the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi, the French church near Piazza Navona, where it still hangs; it was his first major public commission. It shows the moment in the Gospel of Matthew (9:9) when Jesus sees the tax collector at his table and says ‘Follow me’. The physician and art writer Giulio Mancini, writing around 1620, described Caravaggio’s method: ‘a strong light from above with a single window and the walls painted black’. With nothing to bounce light back into the shadows, faces come out bright against near-black, a style called **tenebrism**. Here the beam enters from the upper right, above Jesus and Saint Peter, runs along Jesus’s outstretched hand, which echoes Adam’s in Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam, and lands on the faces at the table; the painted window is not its source. Most art historians see Matthew in the bearded man pointing to himself, though some argue he is the young man at the end of the table. As the [Web Gallery of Art notes](https://www.wga.hu/html_m/c/caravagg/04/23conta.html), the hand bridges a standing group and a seated one.

slides.question: In Caravaggio’s The Calling of Saint Matthew, where does the main beam of light come from?
options: High up on the right, above Jesus
The window painted on the wall
slides.explanation: The beam falls from the upper right, above Jesus and Saint Peter, onto the faces at the table. The painted window is not its source.

slides.alt: Animation, a schematic after Caravaggio’s The Calling of Saint Matthew: a dark room, men at a table, Jesus and Saint Peter at the right; a studio with one high window as its walls turn black; the beam from the upper right along Jesus’s hand to a bearded man; the chapel’s plan.

slides.prompt: Light a face the way the writer Giulio Mancini says Caravaggio did. Find a studio that makes the lit side at least 20 times as bright as the shadow side.
slides.takeaway: Only black walls and a single window do it: nothing bounces light back into the shadows. Pale walls or a second window fill them in and flatten the face.

slides.alt: Caravaggio’s painting: men in 1600s clothes sit at a table in a dark room; at the right, Jesus and Saint Peter stand in shadow, Jesus pointing; a diagonal band of light falls across the wall above them onto the faces at the table.
slides.credit: Caravaggio, photo by Gleb Simonov · CC0

slides.text: A strong light from above with a single window and the walls painted black.
slides.attribution: Giulio Mancini on Caravaggio’s method, Considerazioni sulla pittura, c. 1620

slides.heading: What to look for
items: The beam falls from high on the right, above Jesus.
Jesus’s hand points along it, like Adam’s in Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam.
The bearded man touches his chest, as if to say ‘Me?’
Two men at the left keep counting money.

events.text: The Calling and The Martyrdom are in place
The Inspiration of Saint Matthew, over the altar

slides.question: Giulio Mancini says Caravaggio painted in a room with black walls. What did that do to his pictures?
options: Kept the shadows deep and dark
Hid his models from the street
slides.explanation: Pale walls bounce light into the shadows; black walls hardly do, so the shadow side of a face stays near black. That is tenebrism.
